<div class="container">
    <div class="guide-header">
        <div class="breadcrumb">
            <a href="/">Home</a> / <a href="/guides/">Guides</a> / Wireshark Network Analysis
        </div>
        <h1>Wireshark Network Analysis</h1>
        <span class="new-badge"><i class="fas fa-star"></i> New</span>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem; margin-top: 1rem;">Master packet analysis for
            security investigations, troubleshooting, and network forensics.</p>
        <div class="meta" style="margin-top: 1rem;">
            <div class="meta-item"><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 20 min read</div>
            <div class="meta-item"><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Beginner to Intermediate</div>
            <div class="meta-item"><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Jan 17, 2026</div>
        </div>
    </div>

    <article class="content">
        <img src="/images/guides/wireshark-network-analysis.png" alt="Wireshark Network Analysis Guide"
            class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <p>Wireshark is the world's most popular network protocol analyzer. Whether you're troubleshooting
            connectivity issues, investigating malware communications, or performing network forensics, Wireshark is
            an essential tool in every security professional's toolkit.</p>

        <p>In this comprehensive guide, I'll walk you through everything from basic packet capture to advanced
            filtering techniques used by SOC analysts to investigate security incidents.</p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Why Learn Wireshark?</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Wireshark appears in nearly every SOC analyst job
                description. It's free, cross-platform, and provides unmatched visibility into network traffic.
                Understanding packet-level analysis is crucial for detecting lateral movement, exfiltration, and
                command-and-control communications.</p>
        </div>

        <!-- Table of Contents -->
        <div class="toc">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-list-ul"></i> Table of Contents</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#getting-started">1. Getting Started with Wireshark</a></li>
                <li><a href="#interface">2. Understanding the Interface</a></li>
                <li><a href="#capture-filters">3. Capture Filters (BPF Syntax)</a></li>
                <li><a href="#display-filters">4. Display Filters (Essential Reference)</a></li>
                <li><a href="#protocol-analysis">5. Protocol Analysis Techniques</a></li>
                <li><a href="#security-analysis">6. Security Investigation Techniques</a></li>
                <li><a href="#follow-streams">7. Following TCP/HTTP Streams</a></li>
                <li><a href="#statistics">8. Statistics and Traffic Patterns</a></li>
                <li><a href="#export">9. Exporting Data and Objects</a></li>
                <li><a href="#malware-analysis">10. Malware Traffic Analysis</a></li>
                <li><a href="#best-practices">11. Best Practices for SOC Analysts</a></li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h2 id="getting-started">1. Getting Started with Wireshark</h2>

        <h3>Installation</h3>
        <p>Wireshark is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux:</p>

        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Windows/macOS</span>

Download from https://www.wireshark.org/download.html

# Ubuntu/Debian sudo apt update && sudo apt install wireshark

# Fedora/RHEL sudo dnf install wireshark

# Add user to wireshark group (Linux) sudo usermod -aG wireshark $USER

        <h3>First Capture</h3>
        <p>To capture your first packets:</p>
        <ol>
            <li>Launch Wireshark</li>
            <li>Select your network interface (usually "eth0" or "Wi-Fi")</li>
            <li>Click the blue shark fin icon to start capturing</li>
            <li>Generate some traffic (browse a website)</li>
            <li>Click the red square to stop capturing</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Quick Tip:</strong> Save captures in <code>.pcapng</code>
            format (Wireshark's native format) to preserve all metadata. Use <code>.pcap</code> when sharing with
            older tools.
        </div>

        <h2 id="interface">2. Understanding the Interface</h2>

        <p>Wireshark's interface has three main panes:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Pane</th>
                    <th>Location</th>
                    <th>Purpose</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Packet List</strong></td>
                    <td>Top</td>
                    <td>Shows all captured packets with summary info (time, source, dest, protocol, info)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Packet Details</strong></td>
                    <td>Middle</td>
                    <td>Expandable tree showing protocol layers (Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Packet Bytes</strong></td>
                    <td>Bottom</td>
                    <td>Raw hexadecimal and ASCII representation of selected packet</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Color Coding</h3>
        <p>Wireshark uses colors to quickly identify traffic types:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong style="color: #7CFC00;">Light Green</strong> - HTTP traffic</li>
            <li><strong style="color: #87CEEB;">Light Blue</strong> - UDP traffic</li>
            <li><strong style="color: #FFB6C1;">Light Pink</strong> - TCP traffic</li>
            <li><strong style="color: #FF0000;">Red</strong> - Errors, retransmissions, bad checksums</li>
            <li><strong style="color: #000000; background: #FFFF00;">Black on Yellow</strong> - ICMP traffic</li>
            <li><strong style="color: #90EE90;">Light Green</strong> - DNS traffic</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="capture-filters">3. Capture Filters (BPF Syntax)</h2>

        <p>Capture filters use Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax and <strong>filter packets during
                capture</strong>. This is useful when you know exactly what traffic you need and want to reduce file
            size.</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Important:</strong> Capture filters permanently
            exclude non-matching packets. You cannot recover filtered-out traffic. When in doubt, capture everything
            and use display filters instead.
        </div>

        <h3>Common Capture Filters</h3>

        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Capture only traffic to/from specific host</span>

host 192.168.1.100

# Capture only traffic on specific port port 443

# Capture only TCP traffic tcp

# Capture traffic to specific network net 10.0.0.0/8

# Combine with and/or host 192.168.1.100 and port 80 tcp or udp

# Exclude specific traffic not port 22

# Complex filter: HTTP but not from my IP tcp port 80 and not host 192.168.1.50

        <h2 id="display-filters">4. Display Filters (Essential Reference)</h2>

        <p>Display filters use Wireshark's own syntax and <strong>filter the view of already-captured
                packets</strong>. This is the most common filtering method for analysis.</p>

        <img src="/images/guides/wireshark-filters.png" alt="Wireshark Display Filters Reference"
            class="inline-image" loading="lazy">

        <h3>IP Address Filters</h3>

        <div class="filter-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-network-wired"></i> IP Filtering Examples</h5>
            <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Traffic involving specific IP</span>

ip.addr == 192.168.1.100

# Source IP only ip.src == 10.0.0.5

# Destination IP only ip.dst == 8.8.8.8

# Traffic within a subnet ip.addr == 192.168.1.0/24

# NOT from specific IP !ip.addr == 192.168.1.1 

        <h3>Port and Protocol Filters</h3>

        <div class="filter-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-plug"></i> Port and Protocol Filtering</h5>
            <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Filter by TCP port</span>

tcp.port == 443

# Filter by UDP port udp.port == 53

# Source port only tcp.srcport == 80

# Destination port only tcp.dstport == 8080

# Port range (dynamic ports) tcp.port >= 1024 && tcp.port <= 65535

# Protocol filters http dns tls icmp arp 

        <h3>HTTP-Specific Filters</h3>

        <div class="filter-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-globe"></i> HTTP Traffic Analysis</h5>
            <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># All HTTP traffic</span>

http

# HTTP requests only http.request

# HTTP responses only http.response

# Specific HTTP method http.request.method == “GET” http.request.method == “POST”

# Filter by URL/URI http.request.uri contains “/login”

# Filter by Host header http.host contains “malicious-domain.com”

# Filter by User-Agent http.user_agent contains “curl”

# HTTP response codes http.response.code == 200 http.response.code == 404 http.response.code >= 400 # All errors 

        <h3>DNS Filters</h3>

        <div class="filter-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-server"></i> DNS Analysis Filters</h5>
            <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># All DNS traffic</span>

dns

# DNS queries only dns.flags.response == 0

# DNS responses only dns.flags.response == 1

# Query for specific domain dns.qry.name contains “suspicious.com”

# A record queries dns.qry.type == 1

# TXT record queries (often used by malware) dns.qry.type == 16

# NXDOMAIN responses (domain not found) dns.flags.rcode == 3 

        <h3>TCP Flags and Connection Analysis</h3>

        <div class="filter-box">
            <h5><i class="fas fa-flag"></i> TCP Flag Filters</h5>
            <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># SYN packets (connection attempts)</span>

tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0

# SYN-ACK (connection accepted) tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 1

# FIN packets (connection close) tcp.flags.fin == 1

# RST packets (connection reset/rejected) tcp.flags.reset == 1

# Detect retransmissions (network issues) tcp.analysis.retransmission

# Zero window (flow control issues) tcp.analysis.zero_window 

        <h2 id="protocol-analysis">5. Protocol Analysis Techniques</h2>

        <h3>Decrypting TLS/HTTPS Traffic</h3>
        <p>To analyze encrypted HTTPS traffic, you need either:</p>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Pre-master secret log file</strong> - Set <code>SSLKEYLOGFILE</code> environment variable in
                your browser</li>
            <li><strong>Server's private key</strong> - For RSA key exchange (not ECDHE)</li>
        </ol>

        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Set in your shell before starting browser</span>

export SSLKEYLOGFILE=~/sslkeys.log

# In Wireshark: Edit → Preferences → Protocols → TLS # Set “(Pre)-Master-Secret log filename” to ~/sslkeys.log

        <h3>SMB Analysis</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># All SMB traffic</span>

smb || smb2

# SMB file access smb2.cmd == 5 # Create (file open) smb2.cmd == 8 # Read smb2.cmd == 9 # Write

# Filter by filename smb2.filename contains “password”

        <h2 id="security-analysis">6. Security Investigation Techniques</h2>

        <h3>Detecting Port Scans</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Many SYN packets from single source (port scan indicator)</span>

tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 # Then check Statistics → Endpoints → TCP tab

# RST responses indicate closed ports tcp.flags.reset == 1

        <h3>Detecting Data Exfiltration</h3>
        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># Large outbound transfers</span>

ip.dst != 192.168.0.0/16 && tcp.len > 1000

# DNS tunneling (large TXT queries) dns.qry.type == 16 && dns.qry.name.len > 50

# ICMP tunneling (large payloads) icmp && data.len > 100

        <h3>Detecting Beaconing</h3>
        <p>C2 beacons often show regular intervals. Use Statistics → IO Graph:</p>
        <ol>
            <li>Filter to suspect IP/port</li>
            <li>Set interval to 1 second</li>
            <li>Look for regular spikes (e.g., every 60 seconds)</li>
        </ol>

        <h2 id="follow-streams">7. Following TCP/HTTP Streams</h2>

        <p>One of Wireshark's most powerful features for security analysis:</p>

        <ol>
            <li>Right-click any packet in a conversation</li>
            <li>Select <strong>Follow → TCP Stream</strong> (or HTTP Stream)</li>
            <li>View the complete conversation reassembled</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Pro Tip:</strong> Use "Follow Stream" to see full HTTP
            requests/responses, including POST data, headers, and responses. This reveals credentials sent in
            plaintext, file downloads, and API calls.
        </div>

        <h2 id="statistics">8. Statistics and Traffic Patterns</h2>

        <h3>Essential Statistics Menus</h3>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Menu</th>
                    <th>Use Case</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Statistics → Endpoints</strong></td>
                    <td>Top talkers by IP, MAC, or port</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Statistics → Conversations</strong></td>
                    <td>Traffic between specific IP pairs</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy</strong></td>
                    <td>Protocol distribution breakdown</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Statistics → IO Graph</strong></td>
                    <td>Traffic over time (detect beaconing)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Statistics → HTTP → Requests</strong></td>
                    <td>All HTTP requests by host/URI</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="export">9. Exporting Data and Objects</h2>

        <h3>Export HTTP Objects (Files)</h3>
        <p>Extract files from HTTP traffic:</p>
        <ol>
            <li>File → Export Objects → HTTP</li>
            <li>View all downloaded files</li>
            <li>Save suspicious files for analysis</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Export Other Formats</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>File → Export Specified Packets</strong> - Save filtered packets to new pcap</li>
            <li><strong>File → Export Packet Dissections</strong> - Export as CSV/JSON for SIEM</li>
            <li><strong>File → Export Objects → IMF</strong> - Extract email attachments</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="malware-analysis">10. Malware Traffic Analysis</h2>

        <h3>Common Malware Indicators</h3>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Indicator</th>
                    <th>Filter</th>
                    <th>Significance</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Unusual User-Agent</td>
                    <td><code>http.user_agent contains "python" or "curl"</code></td>
                    <td>Scripted requests, not browsers</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Long DNS queries</td>
                    <td><code>dns.qry.name.len > 50</code></td>
                    <td>Possible DNS tunneling</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Non-standard ports</td>
                    <td><code>tcp.port == 4444 or tcp.port == 5555</code></td>
                    <td>Common RAT/backdoor ports</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Base64 in URLs</td>
                    <td><code>http.request.uri matches ".*[A-Za-z0-9+/]{20}.*"</code></td>
                    <td>Encoded commands/data</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Regular beaconing</td>
                    <td>Use IO Graph</td>
                    <td>C2 check-in intervals</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="best-practices">11. Best Practices for SOC Analysts</h2>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> SOC Analyst Checklist:</strong>
            <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Always work on a <strong>copy</strong> of pcap files, never the original</li>
                <li>Document your filters and findings as you go</li>
                <li>Use <strong>time display format</strong>: View → Time Display Format → UTC Date and Time of Day
                </li>
                <li>Create filter <strong>buttons</strong> for commonly used filters</li>
                <li>Use <strong>coloring rules</strong> to highlight suspicious traffic</li>
                <li>Check <strong>geolocation</strong> of external IPs (Statistics → Endpoints → Map)</li>
                <li>Correlate timestamps with other log sources (SIEM, EDR)</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>Essential Filter Button Set</h3>
        <p>Create these as quick filter buttons (Analyze → Display Filter Expression → Save):</p>

        <pre><code><span class="filter-comment"># C2 Hunt</span>

http.user_agent contains “python” || http.user_agent contains “curl” || http.user_agent contains “wget”

# DNS Anomalies dns.qry.type == 16 || dns.qry.name.len > 50

# Errors Only tcp.analysis.flags || http.response.code >= 400

# Exclude noise !(arp || stp || cdp || lldp)

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Continue Learning:</strong>
            <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">Practice with real malware traffic at <a
                    href="https://www.malware-traffic-analysis.net/"
                    style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">malware-traffic-analysis.net</a> - they provide pcap files
                with analysis walkthroughs. Also check out the Network Forensics section of SANS FOR572.</p>
        </div>
